$comment: Where code stops and text begins.
Two scanners answer this, and everything else believes them:
crates/ruvyxa_bundler/src/ast.rs for the Rust half (imports, the boundary
check, the linker's rewrites) and packages/ruvyxa/runtime/scanner.mjs for the
JavaScript half (the same jobs on the dev and deploy paths). Neither parses;
both walk bytes. That is a deliberate trade and it has one failure mode: a
construct the walk does not know desynchronizes it, and from that point on
the file is read inside out — comment text survives as code and code is
masked away. Nothing downstream can notice, because both halves stay
internally consistent.
Each case below is a shape that has actually broken one of them. Replayed by
the `mod tests` in ast.rs and by tests/packages/ruvyxa/source-scanner.test.mjs.
`code` is a substring that must survive the mask; `text` is one that must
not. Both are checked, because a scanner that blanks everything would pass a
test that only looked for the absence of text.

cases.name: regex holding a quote inside a template interpolation
cases.why: The interpolation is code and may hold a regex; the regex may hold a quote. Reading that quote as a string opener ran to the next quote in the file and inverted everything after it — js-yaml ships this exact line, and the bundle it produced did not parse.

cases.name: regex holding a quote at statement level
cases.why: The same literal outside a template. The outer walk already knew this one; the interpolation walk did not.

cases.name: division is not a regex
cases.why: A `/` after a value is division. Treating it as a regex would swallow the rest of the line and then some.

cases.name: backtick inside a string inside an interpolation
cases.why: A backtick that is string content must not end the template.

cases.name: brace inside a string inside an interpolation
cases.why: A `}` that is string content must not close the interpolation.

cases.name: comment inside an interpolation
cases.why: A brace inside a comment inside an interpolation closes nothing.

cases.name: apostrophe in prose keeps its blast radius to one line
cases.why: An unmatched quote is an apostrophe, not a delimiter. Running to the next quote anywhere in the file is what desynchronizes a scan.

cases.name: nested template literals
cases.why: Template text is not code at either depth, and the inner template must not end the outer one.

$comment: Syntax both compilers must remove before the code is linked.
The emitted bundle is plain JavaScript wrapped in a function. Anything the
language does not allow there has to be gone by then, and both compilers
have to agree on what 'gone' means — the Rust one builds the browser bundle,
and runtime/compiler.mjs builds every server render.
Replayed by the `mod decorator_placement_tests` in
crates/ruvyxa_bundler/src/compiler.rs and by
tests/packages/ruvyxa/erased-syntax.test.mjs.
`@` is not an operator in JavaScript, so a code-position one begins a
decorator. Requiring it to start its own line left the inline form — what
a formatter picks for a short member, and what every minified dependency
has — in the output, where it is a syntax error. The JavaScript compiler
stripped none at all, so a decorated class worked in the browser and threw
on every server render of the same route.
untouched:
const email = "a@b.test"
// reach me @someone
const pattern = /@handle/
const doc = `mention @user here`

$comment: Legal at the top of a module, and Node removes it when it loads one
directly — but a bundled module is wrapped in a function, where `#!` is a
syntax error. Packages that double as executables ship one on their entry
file. The line is emptied rather than deleted so nothing below it moves.
stripped:
#!/usr/bin/env node
export const hit = 1
﻿#!/usr/bin/env node
export const hit = 1
